W7221310695.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance is increasingly strained by interconnected global crises, i.e., pandemics, climate change, armed conflicts, population mobility, and health inequalities, that disrupt healthcare delivery, diagnostic capacity, and laboratory infrastructure. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, whole-genome sequencing, metagenomics, and digital surveillance offer the potential to shift from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence that anticipates resistance threats, although current implementations remain sector-specific, retrospective, and project-funded. Environmental surveillance, particularly wastewater monitoring coupled with genomic epidemiology, provides early warnings at population and ecosystem levels. The future integration of AI across human, animal, and environmental sectors could enable unified One Health intelligence; no such integrated platform is currently operational. This review focuses primarily on bacterial AMR. It examines how global drivers strain surveillance, how genomic, metagenomic, digital, and AI-enabled technologies reshape AMR detection and prediction, and the emerging non-antibiotic therapeutic landscape, including bacteriophage therapy, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based antimicrobials, antimicrobial peptides, microbiota-directed interventions, nanomedicine, host-directed therapies, photodynamic therapy, and vaccines. It then explores how these innovations can be integrated within a One Health framework to support coordinated global preparedness. Addressing the AMR crisis will require not only technological innovation but also equitable implementation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and resilient systems.

W7221512684.abstract: The emergence of autonomous agents based on large language models (LLMs) such as ReAct, LangGraph, AutoGen, or CrewAI — radically transforms the nature of acts produced by artificial intelligence systems. These agents no longer merely generate text: they plan, call system tools, manipulate databases, and execute arbitrary code. This operational autonomy, combined with their demonstrated vulnerability to indirect prompt injection attacks, creates a major evidentiary blind spot: no forensic framework currently exists to legally characterise an illicit act generated by AI before a criminal court. This article proposes a methodological and algorithmic framework for the forensics of autonomous multi-agent systems, structured around three fundamental locks: non-invasive acquisition and cryptographic sealing of the agent's latent state, algorithmic quantification of behavioural deviation, and causal traceability compliant with Article 427 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure and Articles 12 & 13 of the EU AI Act. The project deploys an experimental three-layer software architecture — immutable forensic sensor, behavioural deviation index engine, causal reconstruction and judicial report — and is part of a 36-month doctoral work programme. In my daily practice as a judicial expert in digital forensics, I use classical DFIR tools (EnCase, FTK, Autopsy, Volatility, X-Ways, Axiom, Magnet, IPED) under ISO/IEC 27037. However, when facing autonomous multi-agent systems (ReAct, LangGraph, MCP protocols), these tools become ineffective: they record material alteration but remain blind to the internal probabilistic deliberation of the model. On the legal side, since AI has no legal personality (Article 121-1 of the French Penal Code), judges are powerless before the black box to characterise fault (Article 121-3 of the Penal Code, Article 1242 of the Civil Code), whether the cause is a hostile injection (OWASP LLM01) or spontaneous drift (goal drift). The proposed framework aims to fill this gap by addressing three scientific locks. The first consists in capturing decision-making telemetry (inference contexts, KV-Cache, tool calls) without prohibitive latency, with integrity guaranteed by Merkle trees and certified timestamping (RFC 3161). The second aims to formulate a composite deviation index combining semantic vector divergence (embedding space) and structural violation analysis on action graphs. The third addresses the modelling of the trajectory as causal graphs (Pearl's models) in order to isolate the corrupted input and produce a report admissible in court.

W7221696844.abstract: Abstract Image semantic segmentation, a pivotal task in computer vision, involves partitioning images into meaningful regions for precise pixel-level classification. Although numerous review articles have summarized advances in deep learning-based segmentation, limited attention has been given to systematically examining how architectural innovations interact with the characteristics of benchmark datasets. To address this gap, this review systematically investigates deep learning-based semantic segmentation studies evaluated on four widely adopted benchmarks: Cityscapes, CamVid, PASCAL VOC 2012, and ADE20K. A structured literature search and screening process identified 374 eligible studies, from which representative high-performing models were selected for detailed analysis based on benchmark relevance, architectural novelty, methodological significance, and reported performance. For each study, architectural components, context modeling strategies, attention mechanisms, feature fusion approaches, segmentation performance, limitations, and future research directions were extracted and compared. The synthesis reveals that recent advances are increasingly driven by the integration of multi-scale context aggregation, attention-based feature refinement, transformer-based contextual modeling, hierarchical feature fusion, self-supervised pretraining, and vision-language alignment. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of architectural strategies is strongly influenced by dataset characteristics, including scene complexity, object scale variation, class granularity, temporal structure, and domain diversity. By establishing explicit links between dataset properties and architectural design choices, this review provides a dataset-centric taxonomy and a comprehensive synthesis of emerging design principles for developing robust and generalizable semantic segmentation models.

W7221748231.abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets. We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.

W7221760878.abstract: Diffusion models have been widely used for various generative tasks. However, recent studies have demonstrated that the internal representations learned in the diffusion models' denoising process are insufficiently meaningful, which can hinder the generation performance. To address this, we propose a novel diffusion U-Net architecture enhanced by explicitly aligning the weaker representation from the earlier layer conditioned on higher noise with the better representation from the later layer conditioned on lower noise during training, which we use for the challenging multimodal task of video background music generation. Our diffusion U-Net Self-Representation Alignment (U-SRA) employs an alignment loss to effectively guide our diffusion model to learn good internal representations, thereby enabling it to produce higher-quality symbolic music conditioned on video features. We employ a cross-attention mechanism to synchronize music with video segments. Experiments on a benchmark video-music dataset demonstrate that the proposed U-SRA approach for video background music generation surpasses the state-of-the-art across key evaluation metrics, including video-music alignment and overall music quality.

W7221775329.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.

W7221813772.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

W7222615240.abstract: The increasing complexity of cloud-native infrastructure, characterized by distributed microservices, dynamic workloads, and heterogeneous computing environments, has exposed limitations in conventional fault-management systems. Existing approaches frequently suffer from fragmented fault detection, inaccurate root-cause localization, delayed incident response, and limited autonomous recovery capabilities, compromising infrastructure reliability and operational efficiency. This study proposes an Agentic AI-based Multi-Agent Autonomous Cloud Management Framework (AIC-MAC) to enhance intelligent fault detection, root-cause analysis, and autonomous self-healing in Kubernetes-based cloud environments. The framework integrates six specialized agents responsible for infrastructure monitoring, anomaly detection, root-cause diagnosis, remediation planning, policy enforcement, and recovery verification. It incorporates multivariate telemetry analysis, dependency-aware causal reasoning, evidence-grounded decision-making, and risk-constrained remediation. A controlled experimental methodology is designed using Kubernetes-hosted microservices, observability tools, and fault-injection scenarios. The proposed evaluation assesses fault detection precision, recall, F1-score, root-cause localization accuracy, mean time to detect, mean time to recover, and remediation success rates against conventional monitoring and AIOps baselines. Experimental findings remain pending implementation and validation. AIC-MAC establishes a structured foundation for coordinated, explainable, and safety-aware cloud infrastructure management, with the potential to improve operational resilience and autonomous fault recovery.

W7222852314.abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

W7222871058.abstract: Social media platforms generate large volumes of text where bias, hate speech, and offensive language are often context-dependent; the same expression can carry different connotations depending on the topic being discussed. Existing bias detection methods based on sentiment analysis or surface-level lexical features fail to account for this topical variability. In this work, we propose a context-aware framework for probabilistic bias detection in social media text, built around LLM-driven topic assignment and two complementary scoring strategies. The first approach constructs topic-specific log-likelihood dictionaries ℒt, enabling fine-grained, domain-conditioned bias scoring. The second approach uses a single global log-likelihood dictionary ℒ modulated by a topic-weighted log-prior, offering a scalable and memory-efficient alternative. Both approaches use a predefined taxonomy of 60 topics assigned automatically by a locally-hosted large language model via Ollama. Evaluation on three benchmark datasets covering partisan content, hate speech, and offensive language shows consistent accuracy gains and F1 improvements on two of three datasets; the best configurations achieve F1 scores of 0.8792, 0.9562, and 0.5745 respectively. The results indicate that topic-aware probabilistic modeling can improve sensitivity to context-dependent bias while remaining computationally tractable.

W7222967953.abstract: Synthetic data can support machine-learning research when real observations are scarce, sensitive, expensive, or difficult to share, but synthetic status and dataset size do not establish utility, representativeness, privacy, or fairness. This focused narrative review synthesizes selected research on generation methods, predictive utility, fidelity and diversity, subgroup representation, privacy, fairness-aware generation, recursive training, and large-language-model-generated data. The evidence indicates that suitability is conditional: generated data must preserve information relevant to the intended task, represent important and rare patterns, and be assessed for subgroup disparities and disclosure risks. Results from recursive-training studies further show that repeated reliance on generated data can reduce distributional coverage under some conditions, although the risk depends on the training setup and the availability of real data. Because the reviewed studies use different domains, datasets, methods, and metrics, they do not support a universal ranking of synthetic-data methods. The paper’s central contribution is a proposed integrated evaluation framework that brings together six dimensions—predictive utility, fidelity, diversity, subgroup fairness, privacy, and recursive-data risk—and explains why they should be considered together rather than treated as interchangeable measures. The review is narrative rather than systematic: sources were selected for relevance and influence, no exhaustive screening process was performed, and the synthesis is not a complete census of the field. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated in this paper. The findings support use-case-specific evaluation, transparent reporting, subgroup analysis, documented data lineage, and direct assessment of privacy claims.

W7223031604.abstract: Legal AI research often evaluates large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning tasks under the assumption that relevant facts are already structured and available. This assumption overlooks a prior and practically consequential stage of legal work: fact construction, namely the transformation of incomplete, fragmented, and interactionally disclosed information into coherent factual narratives. This study conceptualizes fact construction as a distinct evaluation layer in legal AI and introduces a practice-grounded framework for assessing it in AI-assisted legal consultation. Rather than proposing a legal advice system or doctrinal rule-matching architecture, we use a role-separated multi-agent workflow consisting of a fact-constrained Litigant Twin, a structured-questioning LegalAider, a NarrativeAgent for factual synthesis, and an Evaluator for factual-alignment assessment. Using 100 de-identified legal clinic consultation records, we evaluate multiple LLMs under rubric-based assessment, comparing generated factual narratives against original human-authored consultation records in terms of factual accuracy, completeness, and consistency. The results show that LLM-based agents can generate usable factual narratives under constrained conditions, particularly when cases are internally consistent, limited to a single dispute, and supported by clear actor-role relationships. However, cross-model evaluator agreement remains moderate, and outlier analysis reveals recurring structural sources of failure, including anonymization-induced referential ambiguity, third-party reporting, multi-episode case complexity, and numerically dense facts. These findings suggest that reliability in AI-assisted legal consultation depends not only on model capability, but also on interaction design, data representation, institutional record-keeping, and human oversight. By treating fact construction as a distinct analytical layer, this article contributes a practice-grounded framework for evaluating responsible LLM integration in legal settings and highlights the need for factual grounding, contestability, and human-supervised review before downstream legal analysis begins.

W7223038609.abstract: Participating in a data space still requires the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) negotiation flow to be hand-coded against each provider's access policy. We present a multi-agent architecture that automates this process using natural language requests. Built on LangGraph over an Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC), the design separates concerns into cooperating agents. The orchestrator's role is to route and plan. The data extraction agent's role is to expose the DSP protocol's three composable tools (catalog discovery, contract negotiation and download). The agent also gates negotiations on the consumers' verifiable credentials, refusing assets rather than fabricating them. Furthermore, there are downstream Machine Learning (ML) and Visualization agents, as well as a final Verification agent, which confirms that the request was actually fulfilled and rechecks the intended operation against the contract's usage policy. In a primary benchmark involving 600 runs, the system achieved 89% task success with zero policy violations when evaluating multi-dimensional policy reasoning with a locally hosted open-weight model. It failed safely through refusal rather than misrouting. The reliability of the system is largely dependent on the phrasing of requests: technical and expert requests succeed up to 98% of the time, whereas casual and under-specified requests succeed 72% of the time. Furthermore, in a secondary evaluation of 600 runs isolating hierarchical geographic access control, the framework successfully blocks 100% of unauthorized regional requests. While the verification agent hallucinates that 1% of these requests, the system logs confirm that no data is ever extracted and the framework simultaneously achieves an end-to-end verified delivery rate of 86% for eligible consumers.

W7223067886.abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security challenge for large language model systems, particularly autonomous large language model-based agents that may interact with external tools, application programming interfaces, and data sources.This study presents a comparative evaluation of five pre-trained transformer models, namely BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT, fine-tuned for binary prompt injection classification.A balanced dataset of 4,224 samples was compiled from 10 publicly accessible corpora containing benign and injection prompts and divided into training (2,956), validation (634), and test (634) sets.The models were trained in the Kaggle environment using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, and a linear warm-up scheduling strategy.On the held-out test set, RoBERTa achieved the highest classification performance, with 97.48% accuracy, 97.52% macro-precision, 97.48% macro-recall, 97.48% macro-F1-score, and 99.64% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.DistilBERT achieved the highest reported throughput of 819.13 samples/s and the lowest per-sample latency of 1.22 ms.Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and SHapley Additive exPlanations-based interpretability analysis were also conducted to examine model differences and influential linguistic features.The findings demonstrate that fine-tuned transformer classifiers can achieve strong performance on the evaluated benchmark dataset while exhibiting different accuracyefficiency characteristics.However, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the evaluated data distribution, as the study does not include independent external datasets or adaptive adversarial attacks.These limitations indicate that further validation is required to establish generalizability and robustness in real-world prompt-injection defense scenarios.

W7223100475.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.

W7223153652.abstract: Modified extensions of the standard cosmological models often introduce complex parameter degeneracies that severely impact sampling convergence of the parameter space while analyzing the model observationally. In this work, we present an accelerated Bayesian inference technique using a Heteroscedastic Deep Ensemble with Monte Carlo Dropout incorporating distance-gated local residual corrections to emulate complex likelihood surfaces and avoid extrapolation beyond the trained region. We demonstrate this methodology on a unified dark energy cosmological model equipped with Finsler geometry. The model is studied using the recent observational datasets, including Cosmic Chronometers (CC), Pantheon$+$SH$0$ES, and DESI DR$2$ BAO measurements. While the conventional sampling procedure struggles with slow mixing of parameter chains ($τ_{max}=1578.3$), the neural network, specially trained densely in high likelihood regions, yields converged and highly resolved posterior distributions of the model parameters without significantly compromising the minimum chi-square value. We further discuss the results for physical inferences and also compare the present dark energy model with $Λ\text{CDM}$ statistically using AIC and BIC.

W7223154847.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a heterogeneous autoimmune disease for which selecting the most appropriate first targeted therapy remains challenging. We integrated ex vivo immune-cell functional assays, targeted proteomics, clinical outcomes, and a three-dimensional (3D) synovial model to identify treatment-associated molecular signatures and evaluate their relationship with subsequent response to Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) or tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi). METHODS: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells and neutrophils from 48 b/tsDMARDs-naïve RA patients were cultured with autologous serum and treated ex vivo with Baricitinib or Etanercept to assess proliferation, adhesion, NETosis, and 92 inflammation-related proteins. The resulting JAKi- and TNFi-modulated protein signatures were subsequently evaluated in pretreatment serum from four independent RA treatment cohorts (n = 223; naïve and non-naïve). Unsupervised clustering was used to identify molecular subgroups, which were related to longitudinal DAS28-CRP outcomes at 3, 6, and 12 months. Logistic regression, neural network, and random forest models were evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation in naïve patients to discriminate treatment-specific 6-month remission outcomes. In a subset of naïve remission achievers, paired baseline and 6-month sera were applied to a 3D synovial micromass model. RESULTS: Ex vivo JAKi and TNFi comparably modulated immune cell functions but induced distinct protein signatures with limited overlap. When evaluated in pretreatment baseline serum, these signatures stratified b/tsDMARD-naïve patients into clusters with different baseline inflammatory profiles and treatment-specific ΔDAS28-CRP. High baseline expression of a drug-specific signature was associated with remission with the corresponding therapy and failure to achieve remission with the alternative treatment. Under repeated nested cross-validation, logistic regression showed the highest mean discrimination among the models, with an AUC of 0.70 (SD, 0.03; empirical 2.5th-97.5th percentile, 0.65-0.75) for distinguishing treatment-specific remission outcomes in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA. In remission achievers, 6-month sera from either therapy significantly reduced synovial lining thickness in 3D micromasses versus baseline. CONCLUSION: Ex vivo-derived JAKi- and TNFi-associated immune-related protein signatures, integrated within a machine-learning framework, showed moderate discriminatory ability for treatment-specific remission patterns in b/tsDMARD-naïve RA and, together with complementary evidence of reduced synovial lining thickness in remission achievers, support further investigation of biomarker-informed selection between JAKi and TNFi as first targeted therapies.

W7223935660.abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive review of existing literature on spelling correction models designed for low-resource languages (LRLs). The research examines how these models handle homophone errors, using Khmer as a case study to highlight challenges in LRLs. Out of 174 academic publications, 54 papers were chosen for detailed study. The review covers various spelling correction models, including traditional, deep learning, and large language models. Traditional methods are affordable to implement but struggle to understand word context properly. Deep learning models (DLMs) provide the best balance between cost and effectiveness for correcting Khmer homophones. Large language models (LLMs) offer the highest accuracy but require significant computational power and may favor languages with more available data. The study also provides a three-stage framework for selecting appropriate models. When data is limited, traditional methods work best for homophone correction. When moderate amounts of data are available, DLMs should be the preferred choice. When both sufficient data and computational resources are accessible, LLMs deliver optimal results. These recommendations offer valuable guidance for researchers who develop spelling correction systems for LRLs, particularly when addressing homophone-related challenges.

W7224004648.abstract: Activation steering offers training-free and dynamic control of target behaviors in large language models, but existing methods can impair general capabilities and require domain-specific intervention designs. We introduce Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS), a unified framework that balances target-behavior control with capability preservation. To make target-behavior improvement and general-capability preservation tractable, we introduce two proxies: log-probabilities of target tokens in model generated responses, and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining the local approximation of the two proxies yields a closed-form solution, enabling lightweight steering without iterative model training or additional inference-time computation. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients achieve effective steering while limiting general-capability loss. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure supports adaptation across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on Qwen and Llama models, CANS achieves comparable or better steering while better preserving MMLU, BBH, and IFEval performance than SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduces HarmBench attack success from $15.50\%$ to $1.75\%$ with a $1.11$-point decrease in average capability. These results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.

W7224109673.abstract: Poor phenotype quality and small cohorts remain major constraints in psychiatric biomarker research, and recent methodological advances increasingly address them. Language models turn clinical text into analysable variables at a scale manual chart review cannot reach. Self-supervised models learn from the unlabelled signals psychiatry already collects. Variant-effect prediction makes molecular interpretation computable, and research agents have generated and experimentally confirmed candidates outside psychiatry. These capabilities act early, on what is measured, what can be learned from it and which candidates are proposed. None of the artificial intelligence capabilities reviewed here yet reaches the stages at which a candidate becomes a clinical test. Producing candidates is becoming cheap while qualifying them is not. This review is organised around that asymmetry rather than by disorder or marker catalogue. It separates the measured characteristic, the prediction model and the intended clinical use, and treats method family as distinct from evidential stage. Across the selected evidence, discrimination is supported more strongly in development data than in independent evaluation, and prospective evidence that model-guided use improves care is scarce. Many reported metrics also address a simpler task than the intended decision: diagnosis instead of differential diagnosis, general prognosis instead of differential treatment benefit. The review proposes a six-stage framework linking intended use, measurement validity, model evaluation, comparative utility and monitored deployment, and places each capability on it, clarifying where methodological progress can accelerate discovery and where conventional clinical validation remains indispensable.

W7224214934.abstract: Available LLMs differ substantially in cost, latency, and capability.Their strengths vary across queries, so the natural question becomes: which model for which query?This is the LLM routing problem.Routing is already used in production, and the academic literature has grown across cascading, bandit, generative, and benchmark threads, each with its own vocabulary, each largely ignoring the others.We argue the field is best read along a single axis: the algorithmic operation the router performs.We organise the recurring operations under four labels.Predictive routers score candidates before their answers are generated.Adaptive routers try a model, observe the outcome, and adjust.Generative routers let an LLM itself reason about the decision.Infrastructure work studies routing rather than performs it, via benchmarks and adversarial analysis.This survey formalises the routing decision under this four-paradigm lens, traces the methodological development of the field, compares assumptions and tradeoffs across paradigms, and identifies open research directions revealed by the taxonomy.A continuously updated reading list lives at https://github.com/wuxingyu-ai/ LLM-Routing.Score every candidate offline, then commit to the argmax no LLM is called before the decision.Predictive Router called trained offline on past data Llama-3 score: 0.92 score: 0.

W7224362461.abstract: Knowledge editing for large language models typically treats a fact update as a replacement in which a new object overwrites the old.Many real-world facts, however, evolve through sequences: the same subject-relation pair maps to different objects across disjoint intervals, each correct within its validity window.Existing temporal-editing benchmarks probe latestvalue or explicit-time recall, so they cannot determine whether an edited model retains a coherent timeline.We introduce TKE-BENCH, a diagnostic benchmark that operationalizes temporal accessibility along three reasoningoriented axes with paraphrased variants.On TKE-BENCH, all evaluated editing baselines collapse on chronologically structured queries, revealing catastrophic temporal interference (CTI).We trace CTI to a geometric property implicit in locate-and-edit methods: mid-layer subject-token keys are nearly collinear across time slices of the same subject, so stacked updates write along one direction and the latest edit overwrites every earlier value.Building on this, we propose CHRONOEXPERT, a temporal mixture-of-experts that stores each time slice in an independent lightweight expert and activates only the matching one at inference, leaving the base model otherwise untouched.Across multiple LLM backbones, CHRONOEXPERT consistently outperforms the strongest editing baselines and stays robust as chains grow longer.

W7224429474.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate when confronted with queries they cannot answer reliably.The root causes are multifaceted, including entity rarity, semantic ambiguity, temporal invalidity, false presuppositions, and other forms of epistemic uncertainty.Existing abstention mechanisms overwhelmingly rely on binary probes trained with manually curated "unanswerable" labels or calibrated confidence scores, both of which presuppose access to negative examples that are expensive to collect and fundamentally incomplete in coverage.We propose FLOW-ABSTAIN, an unsupervised framework that reframes queryaware abstention as density estimation in the model's own latent space.Our method operates in three stages: (1) extracting intermediate hidden-state representations from a curated set of confidently answerable queries, (2) applying PCA-based dimensionality reduction to obtain a compact manifold, and (3) fitting a Masked Autoregressive Flow (MAF) to the resulting representations, yielding an exact, tractable log-likelihood for arbitrary new inputs.At inference time, queries whose latent projections receive low log-likelihood under the learned density are flagged for abstention-without requiring any negative or out-of-distribution training samples.Experiments across three instruction-tuned LLMs (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Llama3-8B-Instruct) and five diverse evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that FLOW-ABSTAIN achieves highly competitive abstention performance among methods with practical inference cost while providing a continuous, interpretable likelihood signal that naturally stratifies query difficulty along cognitive dimensions of unanswerability. 1

W7224456497.abstract: Cultural adaptation, rewriting text for a different cultural audience, requires more than lexical substitution.A model must decide what to change, whether each replacement is locally valid, and whether it preserves the original item's functional role.We formalize this as function-preserving cultural transfer and introduce a dataset, a taxonomy, and an evaluation framework constructed around that principle.CULTURALADAPT-6K identifies 6,000 culturally rich texts in four discourse domains, while the Cultural Rewriting and Adaptation Failure Taxonomy (CRAFT) classifies errors into five categories.To mitigate the Anglocentric priors of current models, our proposed framework anchors each culturally significant item in a Wikidata-linked function frame, capturing its contextual role rather than surface denotation.Across 191,968 adaptations by eight instruction-tuned LLMs, we find that the models that substitute the most are not the ones that substitute best.High localization increases failure exposure, while conservative retention increases validity scores, yet both converge to the same overall functional quality.Current generative models can certainly dress text in a target culture's vocabulary but ultimately cannot reliably preserve the contextual roles the vocabulary is meant to serve.

W7224464424.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to process inputs composed of multiple context units, such as answer options, retrieved passages, or in-context demonstrations.Effective reasoning in such scenarios demands capturing both intrinsic semantics within each unit and the aggregated semantics across units.However, recent efforts typically treat multiple units as a single entangled sequence, ignoring the distinct knowledge within isolated units, which leads to suboptimal performance.To this end, we propose MUA 1 (Multiple Context Units Attention), a dual-view self-attention module that computes a local view for learning unit-specific semantics and a global view to enable bidirectional interaction across units.These two views share projection matrices and are fused by a lightweight input-conditioned gate, while generation proceeds with standard causal decoding.With an optimized implementation, this design achieves efficient fusion of multiple context units and superior information utilization during input encoding at marginal overhead.Experiments on diverse multiple context units reasoning benchmarks, including multiple-choice, multi-hop QA and language understanding tasks, show that MUA consistently improves performance across model scales, exhibits increased robustness to context units reordering, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on key benchmarks.

W7224524270.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly act through tools, APIs, databases, and other stateful environments, where task success depends on external evidence rather than final text alone.Existing reward paradigms face a trade-off: preference and rubric-based feedback are flexible but often weakly grounded, while verifier-based rewards are grounded but typically tied to narrow task-specific checkers.We argue that agentic reinforcement learning needs reward interfaces: mechanisms that explicitly connect task requirements to environment evidence, provenance, and reward aggregation.We introduce Agentic Rubrics, an executable reward-interface view with four components: criteria, evidence acquisition, provenance, and aggregation.This view separates what should be evaluated from how evidence is obtained, audited, and converted into reward.In this case study, Agentic Rubrics augment final environment feedback with process-aware rewards derived from tool traces and state records, yielding modest improvements in task performance and process reliability while revealing domain-dependent limitations.These results support the position that grounded agent learning should treat reward construction as an interface problem, not only as scalar reward modeling. Pure Rubric Verifier Agentic RubricCorrect acceptance: process constraints and state transitions are both verified.

W7224879143.abstract: The growing demand for artificial intelligence systems that are responsive, privacy-preserving, and capable of operating autonomously is driving the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) on edge devices. However, deploying LLMs as the core of agents on devices with limited resources still faces computational and memory constraints. This research develops an LLM-based local agent architecture that runs locally on a Raspberry Pi without relying on cloud services. The system integrates local LLM inference with agentic functions, including intent processing, reasoning, tool invocation, and interaction with hardware via GPIO. Several quantized Small Language Models (SLMs) were evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16 GB of RAM using CPU-based inference. The evaluation included total latency, Time to First Token (TTFT), token generation rate, peak RAM usage, peak CPU utilization, and peak temperature. The results showed significant performance differences among the models. Qwen 2.5 0.5B Q3 produced the lowest total latency of 23.9 seconds, the lowest TTFT of 269.0 ms, and the highest generation rate of 12.1 tokens/s. However, the results indicate that inference speed alone is not sufficient to determine the most suitable model as the core of a local agent. Most models reached peak CPU utilization above 95%, while RAM usage and thermal characteristics varied across configurations. Based on a combination of inference performance and resource usage, models in the 1B–1.7B range specifically LLaMA 3.2 1B Q4, Qwen 2.5 1.5B Q4, and SmolLM 1.7B Q4 show potential as a balanced set of candidates between responsiveness and model capacity. The research results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying LLMs as local agents on low-cost edge devices and provide a basis for selecting models based on a balance between inference efficiency, resource constraints, and agentic capabilities.

W7224975610.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where outputs are grounded in cited sources, yet whether citation presence itself, independent of factual content, shapes model behavior remains poorly understood. We introduce AuthorityBench, a benchmark of 220,564 prompts designed to isolate the effect of citation presence on factual accuracy in large language models. Citations appear passively in prompts, models receive no instruction to trust or defer to them, allowing us to measure whether citation presence alone cause models to give wrong answers. The benchmark independently manipulates two variables: whether the claim is true or false, and whether the accompanying citation is real or fabricated. This yields four conditions tested across four domains (general knowledge, science, law, and medicine), with controlled variation over 40 prompt templates, four venue prestige tiers, and author names from six surname regions. We define hallucination as any response contradicting the ground-truth label, wrongly denying a true claim or wrongly affirming a false one, capturing both the familiar failure of endorsing misinformation and the novel failure of rejecting correct facts under authority pressure; refused responses are excluded from this count. Across all seven models, adding any citation, real or fabricated, increases hallucination above baseline. The effect is largest when a fabricated citation accompanies a true claim: models that answer correctly without a citation are pushed toward wrong answers by the authority signal alone, with hallucination rates rising 3 to 22 percentage points and reaching 35--77% in general knowledge. Legal claims are consistently robust; venue prestige and author demographics have negligible effects; and larger models are no more resistant than smaller ones. All code, datasets, prompt templates, and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/aryank2804/AuthorityBench.

W7225150811.abstract: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

W7225155615.abstract: Current polymers used for carbon capture are limited by their toxic footprint during manufacturing and degradation over time. This review aims to propose a new paradigm for designing membranes for carbon dioxide capture using data-driven approaches to bibliometrics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning with the goal of creating next-generation, sustainable polymers for carbon dioxide capture. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and Bibliometrix will be used to present the most commonly used keywords, people, and countries that are working more on this topic. Furthermore, an exposing of the gaps between the performance of membranes under laboratory settings versus in real world environments will be conducted. AI and machine learning approaches will be investigated to fill these performance gaps. Methods for shifting towards a circular economy with the inverse design of bio based polymers, green fillers, and low carbon, non toxic solvents will be discussed. Finally, the virtual discoveries in the field of polymers for carbon capture will be correlated with the current industrial world to formulate a roadmap for these materials to reach high technology readiness levels for use across the globe.

W7225162656.abstract: An investigation into why a unit of business work did not finish in a distributed operational pipeline crosses several systems of record: schedulers, orchestration engines, warehouses, code repositories and configuration stores. This monograph formulates Contract-Bounded Agent Design (CBAD), a reproducible engineering method for building language-model agents that conduct such investigations within fixed boundaries and can be carried from one pipeline to the next. The method rests on four structural decisions: one narrow, read-only tool per external source, whose description serves as a semantic contract; safety contracts enforced in code, including statement guards, pinned query scopes, payload ceilings and truncation reported with true totals; an explicit failure taxonomy that classifies by meaning on two orthogonal axes, the business stage at which work stopped and the concern that owns the fix; and a named separation between the current state of the work and its historical occurrence. Around the decisions the book sets an ordered investigation runbook, an answer discipline that limits each answer to what the tools returned, and four named design rules: liveness check before trust, best-effort secondary write, partial success by construction and routing by identifier shape. The decisions were derived from two systems developed separately in the author’s own practice as a software engineer, an incident-investigation agent over a workflow orchestration engine and a multi-purpose assistant over a scheduled data pipeline, and the graded convergence of their designs is the principal evidence for the method. The method is positioned against research on tool-using agents, AIOps and failure management, natural-language interfaces to data, software architecture and technical debt. Its procedures are given as checklists, decision tables and rule cards, worked through on a constructed claims-processing pipeline, and the final chapter adds a transfer checklist and a staged adoption path. The book addresses software engineers, site reliability engineers and architects who build, review or adopt agents over production workflow and data systems.

W7225172179.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

W7225242799.abstract: Edge analytics requires continuous model adaptation under tight latency, bandwidth, and confidentiality constraints, yet conventional federated learning can leak sensitive information through shared updates and often struggles under non-IID client data. This study introduces Federated Quantum Machine Learning that transmits privacy-preserving measurement statistics derived from hybrid parameterized quantum circuits rather than raw samples or high-dimensional gradients. Across 50 edge clients over 20 rounds, the proposed method achieves 0.844 accuracy and 0.836 macro-F1 with ECE 0.048, outperforming a classical FedAvg baseline (0.801 accuracy, 0.788 macro-F1, ECE 0.062) while maintaining predictable edge overhead (845 ms average round latency) and compact messaging (3.1 KB average payload per round). Privacy–measurement sweeps demonstrate accuracy saturation with increasing privacy budget, improving from 0.816 at ε = 0.5 to 0.856 at ε = 8.0 under 512 shots, while calibration improves more sharply, with ECE decreasing from 0.068 to 0.046 over the same range. Increasing shot budget from 128 to 2048 consistently increases accuracy under all privacy settings, confirming that measurement variance is a controllable bottleneck for protected learning. Communication analysis shows that statistics-only messaging remains an order of magnitude smaller than gradient-style baselines (33.9 KB average payload per round), and secure aggregation adds bounded overhead (4.8 KB average payload) with a modest utility shift (0.836 accuracy, ECE 0.051). Robustness experiments under severe non-IID drift (severity 0.9) preserve macro-F1 at 0.801 with expectation-based statistics versus 0.772 for histogram-based statistics, and perturbed-client tests show improved stability with robust aggregation, sustaining 0.836 accuracy at 10% perturbed participation compared to 0.824 under naïve aggregation. These results indicate that low-dimensional, privatized measurement summaries enable practical, reliable, and privacy-aligned federated quantum learning on constrained edge infrastructures.

W7225255302.abstract: As autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents transition from passive credit scoring and fraud classification to executing multi-step decision chains in safety-critical financial environments—such as high-frequency algorithmic market making, automated anti-money laundering (AML) asset freezing, cross-border settlement, and dynamic liquidity management—ensuring high precision alongside absolute risk compliance becomes paramount. Traditional statistical validation, backtesting, and empirical stress-testing fall short when confronting the inherent opacity, non-determinism, and infinite state spaces of generative models and deep neural controllers. A single hallucinated transaction parameter set, unauthorized logic branch, or out-of-distribution execution can trigger systemic market instability, severe regulatory non-compliance, or irreversible capital destruction. This paper presents a novel Financial Hybrid Verification Architecture (Fin-HVA) designed to mathematically certify the correctness, policy compliance, and risk bounds of autonomous agent decision sequences prior to market execution. We introduce a neuro-symbolic semantic parser that converts complex natural language reasoning and tool-use parameter arrays into formal Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) formulas and Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) queries. By coupling static SMT reachability solvers with a real-time Runtime Financial Safety Shield (RFSS) and an autonomous evaluator-optimizer repair loop, Fin-HVA guarantees that agent decisions remain strictly bounded within predefined risk envelopes (e.g., maximum drawdown thresholds, capital adequacy ratios, and regulatory compliance constraints). We evaluate Fin-HVA across three simulated high-risk financial domains: automated high-frequency algorithmic liquidity management, dynamic credit line adjustment, and real-time AML transaction interdiction. Our experimental results demonstrate that Fin-HVA completely eliminates safety and compliance violations (0.0% Violation Rate) while maintaining high operational task success rates (>94%) with negligible step latency (<1.3s). This research establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for deploying fully autonomous AI agents within highly regulated financial ecosystems.

W7225256512.abstract: Predicting patient response to cancer treatments remains a challenge due to tumor heterogeneity and complex tumor microenvironments (TMEs). Modern spatial genomics technologies enable gene expression profiling alongside histological frameworks, but comprehensive analysis and clinical translation of these high-dimensionality datasets will benefit from Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This review synthesizes computational approaches that address challenges of spatial data by examining deep-learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for histological feature extraction and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling cell-cell interactions. We then explore the paradigm of Foundation Models that bridge histopathology with transcriptomics to accelerate the identification of spatially resolved biomarkers, improve patient stratification for immunotherapy and targeted treatments, and advance the clinical translation of mechanistic insights derived from the tumor microenvironment.

W7225299146.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by high postoperative recurrence and marked heterogeneity.Conventional imaging and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) are insufficient for precise prognostic assessment and recurrence monitoring.Liquid biopsy, especially circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), can noninvasively reflect tumor genomic alterations and minimal residual disease (MRD), often predicting recurrence 2~5 months earlier than imaging.Radiomics and deep learning can extract high-throughput quantitative features from CT/MRI, reflecting spatial heterogeneity, microvascular invasion (MVI), and the immune microenvironment.Integrating spatial imaging information with temporal molecular information from liquid biopsy into "imaging-genomics" or multimodal fusion models can improve diagnostic accuracy, recurrence risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring.This review systematically summarizes the integrated application of multimodal imaging and liquid biopsy in HCC prognosis and recurrence monitoring.It further emphasizes fusion methodology, including early fusion versus late fusion and their respective advantages and disadvantages, algorithm-specific challenges, HCC etiological heterogeneity (especially NAFLD/MASH-related HCC), controversies and unresolved issues, and specific head-to-head trial designs.Finally, we discuss artificial intelligence, prospective trials, and full-course management.

W7225394258.abstract: Commercialization of lithium metal batteries with high energy density is limited largely due to uncontrolled lithium dendrite growth, poor interfacial resistance of solid-state electrolytes, and inadequate cycle stability of solid-state electrolytes. A new architecture that leverages artificial intelligence to design engineered nanolayer interfaces for solid-state electrolytes enables controlled lithium-ion transport and prevents dendrite propagation in next-generation batteries. To achieve this, the proposed framework combines Multiphysics interfacial modeling with an artificial intelligence optimization module to simultaneously determine the optimal thickness and interfacial parameters for nanolayers to optimize ionic conductivity while minimizing electrochemical degradation. Simulation results show that the engineered interface provides a significantly better electrochemical performance than any existing solid-state electrolyte configuration. The engineered interface provides an ionic conductivity of 1.21 × 10−3 S·cm−1, an improvement of approximately 34.8%, and a decrease in interfacial resistance of 82 Ω·cm² to 46 Ω·cm², a decrease of 43.9%, and a critical current density of 2.1 mA·cm−2 compared to an average critical current density of 1.3 mA·cm−2 demonstrating greater tolerance to dendrites. Long-term cycle testing indicates that the proposed configuration retains 93.4% capacity after 500 cycles, while the conventional interface retains only 79.6% of its capacity when cycled under equivalent conditions. Collectively, these results indicate that the combination of nanolayer engineering and artificial intelligence optimization enables uniform deposition of lithium ions, enhances interfacial stability, and reduces the degree of dendrite-induced degradation. The proposed framework enables large-scale development of safer, long-lasting solid-state lithium-ion batteries and facilitates high-energy-density storage for electric vehicles and large renewable energy systems
